etymology: From Latin exercere, to drive on, to keep busy, to train. Webster 1828: use; practice; the exertion of the body for health or amusement; and the discipline or training of the mind. Paul takes the gymnasium word and applies it to godliness and to the conscience.
biblical_def: Exercise in the New Testament is a training word, borrowed from the gymnasium and used of the soul. Paul’s charge to Timothy is the classic instance: refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness (1 Timothy 4:7), followed by the comparison of returns — bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things. He does not say bodily training is worthless; he says it profits a little and godliness profits in both worlds. The same word describes the maturing of discernment: strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil (Hebrews 5:14). Discernment is not a gift dropped on a Christian; it is a faculty trained by use, and the untrained believer is called a babe in the preceding verse. Hebrews uses it again of affliction: chastening yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11) — the trouble is the trainer. And Paul applies it to himself in Caesarea: herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men (Acts 24:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EXERCISE as use; practice; the exertion of the body for health, or of the mind in study; and, as a verb, to employ, to train, to discipline, to habituate to action. The Latin root means to drive on or keep at work.
webster_full: EXERCISE, n. — Use; practice; the exertions and movements customary in the performance of business.
Practice; performance; as the exercise of religion, the exercise of an office.
Exertion of the body for health or amusement; also, the discipline and training of soldiers.
EXERCISE, v.t. — To employ; to exert; to train by use; to habituate to action; to discipline.
From Latin exercere, to drive on, keep busy — the same root as exercitus, an army, a body of men kept in training.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 4:7
But refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
1 Timothy 4:8
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Hebrews 12:11
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
Acts 24:16
And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
corruption_summary: Sanctification is presented in much modern teaching as something that happens to a passive believer, and 1 Timothy 4:7 answers with an imperative from the training ground: exercise thyself.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a genuine truth being defended by those who resist all talk of effort — that a man contributes nothing to his justification, and that sanctification is the work of the Spirit and not of the flesh. Scripture keeps both. Philippians 2 gives the command and the ground in consecutive verses: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. Paul’s word to Timothy is a gymnasium word, and it assumes repetition, discipline, and days when the thing is not enjoyable. The means are the ordinary ones the Reformed have always named: the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the Lord’s day, the fellowship of the saints. Nobody drifts into godliness.

Hebrews 5:14 removes the other excuse, which is the assumption that discernment is a temperament some Christians have. The senses are exercised to discern good and evil by reason of use, and the writer is rebuking a congregation that ought by this time to be teaching and still needs milk. A believer who cannot tell sound doctrine from plausible error is not suffering from a missing gift; he is untrained, and the training is available. Hebrews 12:11 then adds the part no one chooses: affliction is a trainer too, and the fruit it yields is peaceable but it comes afterward, which is the whole difficulty of enduring it.
roots_summary: Greek gumnazo (G1128), to train naked in the gymnasium, whence the figure in 1 Timothy 4:7 and Hebrews 5:14; askeo (G778) at Acts 24:16, the root of ascetic.
roots_lines: Greek gumnazo (G1128) — to exercise, to train as an athlete; 1 Timothy 4:7, Hebrews 5:14, 12:11.
Greek gumnasia (G1129) — bodily exercise, training; a hapax legomenon at 1 Timothy 4:8.
Greek askeo (G778) — to practise, to exert oneself; only at Acts 24:16, and the root of ascetic.
Greek hexis (G1838) — habit, practice from long use; by reason of use (Hebrews 5:14).
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness, piety; the object of the training in 1 Timothy 4:7-8.
usage: Exercise thyself rather unto godliness (1 Timothy 4:7) — the gymnasium word applied to the soul.
By reason of use have their senses exercised (Hebrews 5:14) — discernment is trained, not issued.
Them which are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11) — affliction as the trainer.

etymology: From with in its older sense of away or against, and draw. Webster 1828: to take back; to recall; to retire; to retreat. Paul uses it for the church’s ordinary discipline of a disorderly brother, and Proverbs uses it for the plain wisdom of not wearing out a welcome.
biblical_def: Withdraw is the New Testament’s word for a measured separation. The command in Thessalonica is explicit and is issued with apostolic authority: we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The offence in that chapter is idleness and busybodying, not heresy, and the aim is stated a few verses later — that he may be ashamed. Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother. The withdrawal is corrective and it stops short of excommunication. Paul gives the same instruction to Timothy concerning teachers who suppose that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5). Proverbs supplies the everyday form of the same wisdom: Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee (Proverbs 25:17). And the word has a solemn use in the other direction, of God withdrawing: Hezekiah was left of God to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart, and the psalmist pleads, Why withdrawest thou thy hand?
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WITHDRAW as to take back; to take from; to recall; to cause to retire or leave; and intransitively, to retire, to retreat, to quit a company or place. The prefix with here carries its ancient sense of away or back.
webster_full: WITHDRAW, v.t. — To take back; to take from; to recall; as, to withdraw a claim or an accusation.
To cause to retire or leave; to remove; as, to withdraw a garrison from a fort.
WITHDRAW, v.i. — To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go away.
The prefix is with in the older sense of away or back, as in withhold, withstand, and the obsolete withsay.
The English noun withdrawing room, contracted to drawing room, preserves the same sense of retiring apart.
scriptures: 2 Thessalonians 3:6
Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.
1 Timothy 6:5
Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.
Proverbs 25:17
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee.
1 Corinthians 5:11

But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
Matthew 18:15
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
corruption_summary: Church discipline has been almost entirely abandoned in the modern church, and 2 Thessalonians 3:6 is the text that shows how far the abandonment goes: even the mildest degree of it, over a matter as ordinary as idleness, is a command.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformers named discipline as one of the marks of a true church alongside the preaching of the word and the right administration of the sacraments, and the reason is visible in these texts. Scripture prescribes a graduated response: private admonition (Matthew 18:15), then witnesses, then the church; withdrawal from the disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6); refusal of table fellowship with the unrepentant professor (1 Corinthians 5:11); and finally putting away from among yourselves that wicked person. Modern congregations have largely kept the first step in theory and abandoned all the rest, with the result that membership means nothing and the unrepentant are confirmed in their sin by the silence of the people who love them least effectively.

The corruption runs in the other direction too, and it is uglier where it occurs. Paul’s controls are as clear as his command: count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother; restore such an one in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted; and the whole aim is that he may be ashamed and repent, not that he may be destroyed. Where discipline is exercised without those controls it becomes the shunning of an offender for the comfort of the offended, and Paul’s word for a man restored in 2 Corinthians 2 is that the church should confirm your love toward him lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Discipline that cannot end in restoration was never the biblical thing.
roots_summary: Greek stello (G4724), to draw in, to shrink from, at 2 Thessalonians 3:6; aphistemi (G868), to stand away from, at 1 Timothy 6:5; Hebrew yaqar (H3365) in the proverb, to make rare.
roots_lines: Greek stello (G4724) — to set, to draw in, to avoid; withdraw yourselves (2 Thessalonians 3:6).
Greek aphistemi (G868) — to stand off, to depart from; from such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5).
Greek ataktos (G814) — disorderly, out of rank; a military word for a soldier out of formation.
Greek entrepo (G1788) — to turn upon oneself, to be ashamed; the stated aim of the withdrawal (2 Thessalonians 3:14).
Hebrew yaqar (H3365) — to be precious, to make rare; literally make thy foot rare in thy neighbour’s house (Proverbs 25:17).
usage: Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6) — discipline commanded for idleness.
From such withdraw thyself (1 Timothy 6:5) — separation from teachers who make merchandise of godliness.
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house (Proverbs 25:17) — the same wisdom in ordinary manners.

etymology: From Latin providere, to see beforehand, to foresee — the same root as providence. Webster 1828: to procure beforehand; to get, collect or make ready for future use. The etymology is the doctrine: God provides because God foresees, and Abraham named a mountain after it.
biblical_def: Provide and providence are the same word, and Genesis 22 is where Scripture makes the connexion unforgettable. Climbing Moriah with the wood on his son’s back, Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham answers, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together (Genesis 22:8). A ram is caught in a thicket, and the father names the place: Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen (Genesis 22:14). The margin gives the sense — the LORD will see, or provide — and centuries later, on that same range of hills, God did provide Himself a Lamb, His own Son. The word also carries a hard human duty. Paul writes: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8). And it governs public integrity: Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men (Romans 12:17) — a Christian is to take thought beforehand for how his conduct will look, not to court approval but because the gospel’s reputation is bound to his.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROVIDE as to procure beforehand; to get, collect or make ready for future use; to prepare; to furnish; to supply; and notes the Latin origin in providere, to foresee. The forethought is in the word itself.
webster_full: PROVIDE, v.t. — To procure beforehand; to get, collect or make ready for future use; to prepare.
To furnish; to supply; followed by with before the thing supplied.
To stipulate previously; as, the law provides for this case.
PROVIDE, v.i. — To take measures beforehand; as, to provide against the evils of a siege.
From Latin pro, before, and videre, to see — the same compound that gives providence and prudence.
scriptures: Genesis 22:8
And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together.
Genesis 22:14
And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.
1 Timothy 5:8
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
Romans 12:17
Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.
Matthew 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
corruption_summary: Providence has been reduced in popular usage to a vague benevolence and in practice to good luck; Scripture’s word means God seeing beforehand and acting accordingly, and Genesis 22 shows it costing Him His own Son.
corruption_paragraphs: God will provide himself a lamb is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, and it is spoken by a father walking uphill with a knife and a son who has just asked the unanswerable question. Abraham does not know how; Hebrews says he accounted that God was able to raise him up even from the dead. What arrives is a ram caught by its horns — a substitute, not a rescue — and the name given the place points forward rather than back: in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen. The Reformed doctrine of providence is not the belief that things generally work out. It is the belief that God governs all His creatures and all their actions to His own ends, and Moriah is the place where that doctrine and the doctrine of substitutionary atonement are shown to be the same thing.

1 Timothy 5:8 will not let the doctrine float free of the household budget. A man who does not provide for his own has denied the faith and is worse than an infidel — language Paul uses nowhere else about a failure of ordinary duty, and he uses it because the unbeliever manages this much by natural affection. Trust in providence is never a substitute for provision; the same God who feeds the ravens gave Joseph seven years to fill the storehouses. And Romans 12:17 extends the forethought outward: a Christian is to arrange his affairs so that they will bear inspection, because things honest in the sight of all men is part of not giving occasion to the adversary.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra’ah (H7200), to see, and so to provide — the verb behind Jehovahjireh; Greek pronoeo (G4306), to think of beforehand, in 1 Timothy 5:8 and Romans 12:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra’ah (H7200) — to see, to look upon, and by extension to provide; Genesis 22:8, 14.
Hebrew YHWH yireh — Jehovahjireh, the LORD will see or provide; the name Abraham gave the mount.
Greek pronoeo (G4306) — to perceive before, to provide for; 1 Timothy 5:8, Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21.
Greek pronoia (G4307) — forethought, provision; the Greek noun standing behind the theological term providence.
Latin providere — to see beforehand; the source of both provide and providence in English.
usage: God will provide himself a lamb (Genesis 22:8) — spoken on the way up Moriah, and fulfilled on it.
If any provide not for his own… he hath denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8) — the household duty stated at full strength.
Provide things honest in the sight of all men (Romans 12:17) — forethought about a Christian’s public integrity.

etymology: From Latin differre, to carry apart, to set asunder. Webster 1828: the state of being unlike or distinct; distinction; disagreement. In Scripture it is a priestly duty — putting difference between holy and unholy — and a gospel abolition: there is no difference.
biblical_def: Difference is a word Scripture uses on both sides of the same coin, and the two uses must be held together. The priest’s charge is to make distinctions: that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean (Leviticus 10:10), spoken immediately after the fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu. Ezekiel repeats it of the restored priesthood: they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean (Ezekiel 44:23). To fail at that is the standing indictment of a corrupt ministry; Ezekiel 22:26 says the priests have put no difference between the holy and profane. Then Paul takes the same word and announces its abolition in one respect only: the righteousness of God by faith of Jesus Christ is unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference (Romans 3:22) — because all have sinned. Jew and Gentile stand on identical ground before God, guilty alike and justified alike. Jude adds a pastoral use that requires wisdom rather than doctrine: of some have compassion, making a difference (Jude 1:22), and the next verse says others are to be saved with fear, pulling them out of the fire.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIFFERENCE as the state of being unlike or distinct; distinction; and also disagreement, controversy, dispute. The Latin means to carry apart, and Scripture’s use is always about what may be carried apart and what may not.
webster_full: DIFFERENCE, n. — The state of being unlike or distinct; distinction; dissimilarity.
The quality that distinguishes one thing from another.
Disagreement; controversy; dispute; as, to compose a difference between parties.
In logic, that by which a species is distinguished from all others of the same genus.
From Latin differre, to carry apart — the same verb that gives defer in the sense of putting off.
scriptures: Leviticus 10:10
And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;
Ezekiel 44:23
And they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean.
Romans 3:22
Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference:
Jude 1:22
And of some have compassion, making a difference:
Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
corruption_summary: Romans 3:22 is lifted out of its argument to abolish every distinction, including the ones Leviticus 10:10 requires; the verse says there is no difference in guilt and in the way of justification, and it says nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no difference is the conclusion of an argument that has just proved every mouth stopped and all the world guilty before God, and the reason is supplied in the very next clause: for all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God. That is where the levelling operates — in guilt, and therefore in the way of salvation, which is by grace through faith for Jew and Greek alike. It is not a statement that all religions are one, that moral distinctions are illusory, or that the church must not distinguish holy from profane. Paul who wrote it also wrote what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and be ye not unequally yoked. The gospel abolishes the distinction of merit, not the distinction of holiness.

Leviticus 10:10 is given in the shadow of a judgment, immediately after Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and died, and immediately before the prohibition of wine to the priests on duty. The connexion is deliberate: the ministry exists to teach a people to tell the difference, and a minister with a fogged head cannot do it. Ezekiel names the collapse of that function as one of the reasons Jerusalem fell. Wherever the pulpit stops distinguishing — between the church and the world, the converted and the unconverted, worship God commanded and worship He did not — the people lose the faculty, and Hebrews says the senses are trained by use. A congregation that is never taught to discern will not learn it elsewhere.
roots_summary: Hebrew badal (H914), to divide, to separate, to make a distinction; Greek diastole (G1293), a distinction, at Romans 3:22; diakrino (G1252), to judge between, at Jude 22.
roots_lines: Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, separate, distinguish; the same verb used of God dividing light from darkness (Genesis 1:4).
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) and chol (H2455) — holy and common or profane; the first pair of Leviticus 10:10.
Greek diastole (G1293) — a distinction, a difference; Romans 3:22, 10:12, 1 Corinthians 14:7.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to separate, to discriminate, to judge between; Jude 22, and of doubting in James 1:6.
That badal is the verb of Genesis 1 is significant: distinguishing is a creational act before it is a priestly one.
usage: That ye may put difference between holy and unholy (Leviticus 10:10) — the priest’s standing duty.
There is no difference (Romans 3:22) — the levelling of all men in guilt and in grace.
Of some have compassion, making a difference (Jude 1:22) — pastoral wisdom that treats cases unlike.

etymology: From over and sight. Webster 1828 gives two nearly opposite senses: superintendence, watchful care; and an overlooking, an omission or mistake. The English word thus contains both the elder’s duty and the failure of it, which is a small accident of language worth noticing.
biblical_def: Oversight is Peter’s word for the eldership, and the verse in which it stands is the fullest job description of the office in Scripture: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2). Three contrasts, and each names a real temptation — the man who serves because he cannot get out of it, the man who serves for money, and the man who serves to be somebody, addressed in the next verse as neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. The Greek verb is the one behind bishop, which is why the New Testament uses elder, bishop, overseer, and pastor of a single office; Peter, writing as a fellow elder, uses the shepherd word and the overseer word in the same sentence. Paul does the same at Miletus, calling for the elders of Ephesus and telling them the Holy Ghost has made them overseers, to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood. The Old Testament uses the word of the men set over the temple work — the Levites who had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OVERSIGHT as superintendence, watchful care, as of an overseer; and also a mistake, an omission, an inadvertency — the two senses arising from the two ways one may look over a thing.
webster_full: OVERSIGHT, n. — Superintendence; watchful care; as, the oversight of a school or of a flock.
Mistake; error; omission; an overlooking; as, this fault was an oversight.
OVERSEER, n. — One who overlooks; a superintendent; and in Scripture, a bishop or elder (Acts 20:28).
The double sense arises from the two ways of looking over a thing — watching it, or passing over it without seeing.
The New Testament uses episkopos, overseer or bishop, and presbuteros, elder, of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7).
scriptures: 1 Peter 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Acts 20:28
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Titus 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Titus 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
Hebrews 13:17

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: The identification of elder, bishop, and overseer as one office is the plainest exegetical ground of Presbyterian and congregational polity against the threefold hierarchy, and Titus 1:5-7 makes the interchange within two verses.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul tells Titus to ordain elders in every city, and then two verses later gives the qualifications for a bishop, describing the same men. At Miletus he summons the elders of the church and tells them the Holy Ghost has made them overseers and charges them to feed — that is, to pastor — the flock. Peter, calling himself an elder, does the same in one verse. Three terms, one office, and no trace in the New Testament of a bishop set over a college of presbyters. The later development of the monarchical episcopate, and the Roman papacy built upon it, are not found in the apostolic writings, and this is why the Reformed churches restored a plurality of elders in each congregation.

The polity argument matters less pastorally than the three temptations Peter names, which the office attracts in every generation. Not by constraint, but willingly — against the man serving out of guilt or because nobody else would, whose ministry becomes an endurance. Not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind — against the man for whom it is a living, a caution Paul repeats to Timothy and Titus, and one that the modern celebrity ministry with its book deals and conference fees should read slowly. And neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock — against the domineering elder, whose sin our Lord addressed by washing feet. Hebrews adds the flock’s side: they watch for your souls and must give account, so let them do it with joy.
roots_summary: Greek episkopeo (G1983), to oversee, to look upon, at 1 Peter 5:2; episkopos (G1985), an overseer or bishop; presbuteros (G4245), an elder; poimaino (G4165), to shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, to take the oversight; 1 Peter 5:2 and Hebrews 12:15.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, bishop; Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; used of the same men at Acts 20:17 and Titus 1:5.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed; feed the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2).
Hebrew peqiddah and melakah — the Levites who had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God (Nehemiah 11:16).
usage: Taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly (1 Peter 5:2) — the office and its first temptation.
The Holy Ghost hath made you overseers (Acts 20:28) — elders, overseers, and shepherds as one office.
They watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Hebrews 13:17) — the weight the oversight carries.

etymology: From Old French espier, to watch, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: a person sent secretly into an enemy’s camp to inspect their works and ascertain their designs. Scripture records three famous sets of spies, and their reports decide the fate of a generation, a city, and a harlot’s household.
biblical_def: The spies of Scripture are sent three times to memorable effect. At Kadeshbarnea God commands it: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them (Numbers 13:2). Twelve rulers went; ten came back with the fruit in their hands and this conclusion: We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we (Numbers 13:31). The land was as good as reported and the giants were as real as reported; the difference between the ten and the two was the clause about God, and a nation died in the wilderness over it. Forty years later Joshua, who had been one of the two, sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho (Joshua 2:1) — and this time the report is that the inhabitants’ hearts had melted. Rahab hid them, made her confession, and hung the scarlet line, and Hebrews puts her among the faithful because she had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31). The third set is Moses’ sons of Israel remembering: the men that Moses sent to spy out the land… died by the plague before the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPY as a person sent into an enemy’s camp to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs, and communicate intelligence; and, in a secondary sense, one who watches the conduct of others.
webster_full: SPY, n. — A person sent into an enemy’s camp or country to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs, and communicate such intelligence.
One who watches the conduct of others — used in a bad sense of a secret and malicious observer.
SPY, v.t. — To gain sight of; to discover at a distance or in concealment; to explore; to view or examine secretly.
Joseph accuses his brethren of being spies three times in Genesis 42, using the charge as a means of testing them.
Galatians 2:4 speaks of false brethren brought in privily, who came in privily to spy out our liberty — the bad sense Webster records.
scriptures: Numbers 13:2
Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them.
Numbers 13:31
But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.
Numbers 13:33
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
Hebrews 11:31
By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.
Numbers 14:11
And the LORD said unto Moses, How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them?
corruption_summary: The report of the ten spies is usually filed under pessimism or poor morale, and Scripture files it under unbelief — a distinction that changes both the diagnosis and the cure.
corruption_paragraphs: The ten did not lie about the land or the giants. Their facts were the same facts Caleb and Joshua had, and their conclusion, considered as military assessment, was correct: Israel could not take those cities. The error was in the frame. We be not able is a true sentence in a universe with no God in it, and God’s own verdict on the episode names what was missing: how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them? Unbelief is not usually a denial of evidence; it is the omission of God from an otherwise accurate calculation. The pastoral consequence is considerable, because the standard modern remedies for discouragement — better morale, positive framing, confidence-building — address the symptom and leave the omission in place.

Rahab supplies the counter-case, and it is the more remarkable for who she was. A Canaanite harlot in a doomed city had heard the same reports the spies brought back forty years earlier — the Red Sea, Sihon, Og — and drew the opposite conclusion: the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath. She acted on it at the risk of her life, hid the men, and hung out the scarlet line, and she is named in Hebrews 11, in James 2, and in the genealogy of Christ. The same evidence produced a generation of carcases in the wilderness and one converted household inside the walls. What made the difference was faith, and faith is a gift.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragal (H7270), to go about on foot, to spy out, from regel, a foot; tur (H8446), to search out, at Numbers 13:2; Greek kataskopos (G2685) at Hebrews 11:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to spy out, to go about as a footman or slanderer; Joshua 2:1, Genesis 42:9.
Hebrew tur (H8446) — to search out, to explore; the verb of Numbers 13:2, and of the Preacher searching out wisdom.
Hebrew regel (H7272) — a foot; the root of ragal, since a spy goes on foot.
Greek kataskopos (G2685) — a spy, a scout; a hapax legomenon at Hebrews 11:31.
Greek kataskopeo (G2684) — to spy out; Galatians 2:4, of false brethren spying out Christian liberty.
usage: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:2) — a mission God Himself commanded.
We be not able to go up… for they are stronger than we (Numbers 13:31) — accurate arithmetic with God left out.
She had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31) — a Canaanite’s faith commended in the roll of the faithful.

etymology: From Latin prolongare, to lengthen out. Webster 1828: to lengthen in time; to extend the duration of; to put off to a distant time. Scripture uses it of the days a covenant people may live in the land, and once, astonishingly, of the days of a Servant who has just been put to death.
biblical_def: Prolong is a covenant word before it is anything else. Moses attaches it to obedience: Ye shall walk in all the ways which the LORD your God hath commanded you, that ye may live, and that it may be well with you, and that ye may prolong your days in the land which ye shall possess (Deuteronomy 5:33) — and the fifth commandment carries the same promise, which Paul calls the first commandment with promise. Proverbs states it as a general rule of God’s ordinary government: The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened (Proverbs 10:27). Then Isaiah uses the word in the one place where it cannot mean what it usually means. In the middle of the account of the Servant’s death and burial: it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand (Isaiah 53:10). A man whose soul has been made an offering for sin, who was cut off out of the land of the living, will nevertheless see His seed and prolong His days. That is the resurrection announced in a prophecy of the crucifixion, and the two halves stand in one verse.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROLONG as to lengthen in time; to extend the duration of; to put off to a distant time; and to lengthen in space or extent. Only the temporal senses appear in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: PROLONG, v.t. — To lengthen in time; to extend the duration of; as, to prolong life.
To lengthen; to draw out in time by delay; to put off to a distant time.
To extend in space or length — a sense Webster marks as less common.
From Latin pro, forth, and longus, long — to draw forth at length.
The Authorized Version also uses prolongeth and prolonged, chiefly in Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 5:33
Ye shall walk in all the ways which the LORD your God hath commanded you, that ye may live, and that it may be well with you, and that ye may prolong your days in the land which ye shall possess.
Proverbs 10:27
The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened.
Isaiah 53:10

Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.
Isaiah 53:11
He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.
Ephesians 6:2
Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;)
corruption_summary: Isaiah 53:10 is one of the strongest resurrection texts in the Old Testament, and critical readings that make the Servant a personified Israel or a merely martyred prophet cannot account for the clause about prolonged days after an offering for sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The corporate reading of the Servant — that he is Israel personified — runs aground repeatedly in this chapter, and nowhere harder than here. The Servant is cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of my people, which distinguishes Him from them; He makes His grave with the wicked and with the rich in His death; and then, having been made an offering for sin, He shall see his seed and shall prolong his days. A dead man does not prolong his days, and a nation is not made an offering for its own transgression. Nor does the martyred-prophet reading survive the next verse, where by His knowledge He shall justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities — which is substitution and justification in a sentence written seven centuries before Calvary.

The covenant promise attached to obedience needs the same care as the proverbs of plenty. Deuteronomy 5:33 and Proverbs 10:27 describe how God ordinarily governs a world, and the fifth commandment carries the promise Paul repeats to the Ephesians. They are not a guarantee that the godly always outlive the wicked; Abel died first, Josiah at thirty-nine, and Stephen young. The Reformed reading takes them as the ordinary rule of God’s providence, fulfilled with perfect exactness in the life to come, where the days prolonged are without end. And the ground of that hope is the very Servant of Isaiah 53, whose own days were prolonged out of a borrowed tomb.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak (H748), to be long, to prolong; the same root as erek appayim, slow to anger, literally long of nostrils.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H748) — to be long, to prolong, to lengthen; Deuteronomy 5:33, Proverbs 10:27, Isaiah 53:10.
Hebrew erek (H750) — long, patient; the adjective of the same root, used in slow to anger.
Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed, offspring; he shall see his seed (Isaiah 53:10).
Hebrew asham (H817) — a trespass or guilt offering; when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin.
Greek makrochronios (G3118) — long-lived; that thou mayest live long on the earth (Ephesians 6:3), quoting the fifth commandment.
usage: That ye may prolong your days in the land (Deuteronomy 5:33) — the covenant promise attached to obedience.
The fear of the LORD prolongeth days (Proverbs 10:27) — God’s ordinary government of a world.
He shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10) — resurrection inside a prophecy of the cross.

etymology: From Old English strypan, to plunder, to despoil. Webster 1828: pulled or torn off; deprived; made naked; robbed. The Authorized Version also keeps the older form stript. Scripture uses it of Joseph, of Job, of the man on the Jericho road, and of Christ before the soldiers.
biblical_def: Stripped in Scripture marks the moment a man is reduced to nothing, and the same word runs from Genesis to the passion. Joseph’s brothers begin with the coat: when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him (Genesis 37:23) — the token of the father’s love removed before the pit and the sale. Job uses it of God’s dealing with him: He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head (Job 19:9), and it is three verses before I know that my redeemer liveth. Our Lord’s parable puts it on the Jericho road: a certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead (Luke 10:30) — and the priest and the Levite pass a man who has nothing left to identify him. Then the word reaches its end at the Praetorium: they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe (Matthew 27:28), and afterward they took the robe off and led Him away to be crucified. He who stripped Himself of the form of God was stripped by soldiers, and the garments were parted and gambled for at the foot of the cross.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STRIP as to pull or tear off, as a covering; to deprive of a covering; to make naked; to deprive; to divest; to rob or plunder. All the senses are violent, and Scripture’s uses are all involuntary.
webster_full: STRIP, v.t. — To pull or tear off, as a covering; to deprive of a covering; to make naked.
To deprive; to divest; to bereave; as, to strip a man of his possessions or his honors.
To rob; to plunder; to pillage; as, robbers strip a house.
STRIPPED, STRIPT, pp. — Deprived; made bare; plundered.
The Authorized Version uses both spellings; stript at Genesis 37:23 and stripped at Luke 10:30 and Matthew 27:28.
scriptures: Genesis 37:23
And it came to pass, when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him;
Job 19:9
He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head.
Luke 10:30
And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
Matthew 27:28
And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe.
Philippians 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture never sentimentalizes the stripping of a man, and that the God who permits it is the God who was stripped Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What deserves recovery is Job 19:9 and its position. He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head — Job says it of God, not of the Sabeans or the Chaldeans, and Scripture never corrects him for it. He had already said, the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD, and the book’s narrator says he sinned not nor charged God foolishly. The comfort available to a stripped believer is not that God had nothing to do with it. It is that God had everything to do with it and is nevertheless his Redeemer, which is precisely what Job says three verses later, standing in the ashes with nothing left.

The Jericho road and the Praetorium belong together. In the parable the stripped man is passed by a priest and a Levite, and the neighbour turns out to be the despised Samaritan — a story our Lord told in answer to a lawyer looking for a boundary on the command to love. In Matthew 27 the stripped man is Christ Himself, mocked with a scarlet robe and a reed and a crown of thorns, and the passers-by wagged their heads. Philippians 2 says He had already stripped Himself before any soldier touched Him: made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. Nothing was taken from Him that He had not first laid down, and that is the difference between His stripping and every other in Scripture.
roots_summary: Hebrew pashat (H6584), to strip off, to flay, to make a raid; Greek ekduo (G1562), to strip off clothing; kenoo (G2758), to empty, in Philippians 2:7.
roots_lines: Hebrew pashat (H6584) — to strip off, to flay, and also to make a raid; Genesis 37:23, 1 Samuel 19:24.
Greek ekduo (G1562) — to take off, to strip; Matthew 27:28, 31, and Luke 10:30.
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, to make void; made himself of no reputation (Philippians 2:7).
Hebrew ketoneth passim — the coat of many colours, or of long sleeves, stripped from Joseph.
Greek himation (G2440) — an outer garment; the raiment parted among the soldiers at the cross (Matthew 27:35).
usage: They stript Joseph out of his coat (Genesis 37:23) — the token of a father’s love taken first.
He hath stripped me of my glory (Job 19:9) — a sufferer naming God as the agent and still calling Him Redeemer.
They stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe (Matthew 27:28) — the last stripping, and a willing one.

etymology: An imitative word, from Middle English hissen, formed from the sound itself. Webster 1828: to make a sound by driving the breath between the tongue and the upper teeth; to express contempt or disapprobation by hissing. In the prophets it is the standing sound of the nations passing a ruined city.
biblical_def: Hiss in the Old Testament is the noise of astonished scorn, and the prophets use it as a fixed formula for what a nation becomes under judgment. Jeremiah pronounces it over Judah: God will make this land an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations (Jeremiah 25:9), and again of the exiles, a curse, and an astonishment, and an hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations whither I have driven them (Jeremiah 29:18). Solomon had been warned of it at the dedication of the temple itself: if Israel forsook the LORD, at this house, which is high, every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss (1 Kings 9:8). Micah says the same to a people keeping the statutes of Omri (Micah 6:16), and Hezekiah’s reformation begins with the admission that God has delivered them to trouble, to astonishment, and to hissing, as ye see with your eyes (2 Chronicles 29:8). Zephaniah turns the sound on Nineveh: This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation… every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand (Zephaniah 2:15). The same verb has one wholly different use: God hisses for the nations, whistling for them as a beekeeper whistles for bees.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HISS as to make a sound by driving the breath between the tongue and the upper teeth; to express contempt or disapprobation by hissing; and as a noun, the sound so made, or an expression of contempt.
webster_full: HISS, v.i. — To make a sound by driving the breath between the tongue and the upper teeth, as the serpent does.
To express contempt or disapprobation by hissing; as, the audience hissed the performance.
HISS, v.t. — To condemn by hissing; to explode.
HISS, n. — The sound made by propelling the breath between the tongue and upper teeth; an expression of contempt or scorn.
The word is imitative in every language that has it, which is why Webster offers no further etymology.
scriptures: 1 Kings 9:8
And at this house, which is high, every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, Why hath the LORD done thus unto this land, and to this house?
Jeremiah 25:9

Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations.
Jeremiah 29:18

And I will persecute them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, and an astonishment, and an hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations whither I have driven them:
Micah 6:16

For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people.
Zephaniah 2:15

This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God cares about the reputation of His own name among the nations, and that the hissing of the heathen over a ruined church is a real element of the judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What wants recovering is the question the passers-by ask in 1 Kings 9:8: Why hath the LORD done thus unto this land, and to this house? The hissing is not merely the mockery of enemies; it is a public verdict on a people who bore God’s name and were destroyed. Ezekiel says God acted for His holy name’s sake, which Israel had profaned among the heathen, and Paul quotes Isaiah at the Jews of his own day: the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you. A church whose conduct makes the world hiss has done more damage than it can measure, and no amount of internal encouragement repairs it. Discipline exists partly for this reason.

Zephaniah’s sentence over Nineveh names the disposition that earns the hissing, and it is not chiefly cruelty: the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me. That last clause is a divine title — I am the LORD, and there is none else — taken into the mouth of a city. Nineveh had repented once under Jonah and had returned to this. Babylon says the same in Isaiah 47:8. Self-sufficiency uttered in the language of deity is the sin the prophets punish with derision, and derision is the fitting punishment, because the claim was ridiculous all along. He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh.
roots_summary: Hebrew sharaq (H8319), to hiss or whistle, and the noun shereqah (H8322), a hissing; the same verb is used of God whistling for the nations.
roots_lines: Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss, to whistle; used of scorn at Jeremiah 19:8 and of God summoning nations at Isaiah 5:26.
Hebrew shereqah (H8322) — a hissing, an object of derision; the noun in the prophetic formula.
Hebrew shammah (H8047) — astonishment, horror, desolation; its constant companion in the formula.
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach; the third member at Jeremiah 29:18.
Isaiah 7:18 uses the same verb of God hissing for the fly of Egypt and the bee of Assyria — a beekeeper’s whistle for armies.
usage: Every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss (1 Kings 9:8) — warned at the temple’s dedication.
An astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations (Jeremiah 25:9) — the prophetic formula of judgment.
I am, and there is none beside me (Zephaniah 2:15) — the boast that earned the hissing.

etymology: From Arabia, Hebrew Arab, connected with a root meaning desert or steppe — and by a homonym, evening or darkness. Webster 1828 defines ARABIAN as a native of Arabia. They appear in Scripture as desert tribes on Judah’s southern flank, as tributaries, as raiders, and at Pentecost.
biblical_def: The Arabians in Scripture are the desert peoples south and east of Judah, and their appearances are brief and telling. They brought tribute to Jehoshaphat and to Solomon, and then turned raider under a wicked king: the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines, and of the Arabians, that were near the Ethiopians (2 Chronicles 21:16), and they carried away his substance and his sons. Under a good king the reverse: God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims (2 Chronicles 26:7). Geshem the Arabian is one of the three named opponents of Nehemiah’s wall, joining Sanballat and Tobiah in mockery and then in a plot. Isaiah uses them for the completeness of Babylon’s desolation — neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there (Isaiah 13:20), meaning not even a nomad who pitches anywhere will camp on that ground. And then the New Testament: among the tongues heard at Pentecost were Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God (Acts 2:11) — the last nation named in the list. Paul went into Arabia after his conversion and returned to Damascus (Galatians 1:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ARABIAN as a native of Arabia, and ARABIC as pertaining to Arabia or its language; the older geographies divide the country into Arabia Petraea, Deserta, and Felix, distinctions the King James translators’ contemporaries would have known.
webster_full: ARABIAN, n. — A native of Arabia; an Arab.
ARABIAN, a. — Pertaining to Arabia or its inhabitants.
The Hebrew Arab is connected with a root meaning a desert or steppe, whence Arabah, the desert plain of the Jordan valley.
The classical division was Arabia Petraea (about Petra), Arabia Deserta, and Arabia Felix — the last being the fertile south, Sheba’s country.
Galatians 4:25 places Sinai in Arabia, which is why Paul’s journey there after conversion has often been read as more than geography.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 21:16
Moreover the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines, and of the Arabians, that were near the Ethiopians:
2 Chronicles 26:7
And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims.
Isaiah 13:20
It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there.
Acts 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Galatians 1:17
Neither went I up to Jerusalem to them which were apostles before me; but I went into Arabia, and returned again unto Damascus.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Acts 2:11 — that the Arabians are on the Pentecost list, and that no people group has ever been outside the reach of the gospel’s first day.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery here is the list in Acts 2. Luke names Parthians, Medes, Elamites, dwellers in Mesopotamia, Judaea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya, Rome, Cretes, and Arabians — and the Arabians come last, as if the roll were being extended to the edge of the known desert on purpose. The tongues of Pentecost were the reversal of Babel: at Babel God confounded the language of all the earth and scattered them, and at Pentecost He gave the wonderful works of God in every man’s own tongue and gathered them. Any account of missions that treats a people as unreachable has forgotten which list they are on.

There is a second, quieter matter in Galatians 1:17. Paul, newly converted and burning to preach, did not go up to Jerusalem to the apostles; he went into Arabia. Sinai is in Arabia by his own reckoning in Galatians 4:25, and the man who would write Romans spent that interval alone with God and the Scriptures he had known all his life and now understood. Nothing in the text tells us what he did there. What it does show is that the most gifted mind the church has ever had was not hurried into the pulpit, and that a period of obscurity between conversion and ministry has apostolic precedent.
roots_summary: Hebrew Arab (H6152), Arabia, and Arbi (H6163), an Arabian; connected with arabah (H6160), a desert plain; Greek Arabia (G688) and Araps (G690).
roots_lines: Hebrew Arab (H6152) — Arabia; the desert country south and east of Palestine.
Hebrew Arbi (H6163) — an Arabian; used of Geshem the opponent of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:19).
Hebrew arabah (H6160) — a desert plain, a steppe; the Arabah of the Jordan rift, from the same root.
Greek Araps (G690) — an Arabian; a hapax legomenon at Acts 2:11.
Greek Arabia (G688) — Arabia; Galatians 1:17 and 4:25, where Sinai is placed in it.
usage: The Arabians, that were near the Ethiopians (2 Chronicles 21:16) — raiders stirred up against a wicked king.
Neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there (Isaiah 13:20) — desolation so complete that a nomad will not camp on it.
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues (Acts 2:11) — the last nation on the Pentecost roll.
